stories.headline: India's richest family launches the country's biggest-ever stock market debut: Jio Platforms opens to the public today
stories.dek: Mukesh Ambani's cheap-internet company hopes to raise up to £2.4bn. Big global funds have already signed up, but the price tag is lower than first hoped.
stories.caveman: An IPO is when a private company sells its shares to the public for the first time. Jio Platforms, the internet and phone company of billionaire Mukesh Ambani (India's second-richest man), opens its IPO to ordinary investors on Wednesday Oct. 21, and it closes on Friday. Jio wants to raise up to 302 billion rupees (about £2.4bn) at a price of 1,065 to 1,119 rupees per share. At the top price, the whole company would be worth 10.3 trillion rupees, making it India's fourth-biggest company. Before the public sale, 212 big "anchor" investors, including BlackRock, Fidelity and Singapore's state fund, already bought in. Jio started in 2016 and grabbed 100 million users in under six months by starting a price war that made mobile internet cheap for millions of Indians. Meta and Google invested in it in 2020. Its parent company is even offering its 400,000+ staff a discount to buy shares.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a test of whether investors still want Indian stocks: the main Nifty 50 index is down more than 12% this year. A big success could pull more money into India; a flop would add to the gloom.
stories.camps: Fans: Jio changed India by making data cheap, has hundreds of millions of users, and plans to grow into AI and cloud computing. Skeptics: the valuation is far below the more than £110bn talked about in the summer, the Indian market is falling, and some critics worry about how much of India's economy one family controls.
stories.image_alt: Mukesh Ambani, chairman of Reliance Industries, speaking at a business summit
stories.image_credit: Photo: Amit Dave/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a company sells shares on the stock market.
How much the whole company is said to be worth.
Big investors who promise to buy shares before the public sale, to show confidence.
India's money. Roughly 125 rupees equal one British pound.
A list of 50 big Indian companies; its level is a scorecard for India's stock market.
When companies keep cutting prices to steal customers from each other.

stories.headline: A cheese importer sues Trump over his 50% tariffs on Canada, saying a 96-year-old law can't be used this way
stories.dek: The case targets tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, cheese and more. The same legal group already beat Trump's 'reciprocal' tariffs at the Supreme Court.
stories.caveman: A tariff is a tax on goods brought in from another country. In July, President Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — a law that had never been used to set a tariff before — to put 50% tariffs on many Canadian products, saying Canada treats US goods unfairly. The tariffs started Aug. 22, and Canada hit back with its own. On Tuesday, Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey food importer, sued in the US Court of International Trade. It says it now pays about $40 million a year in tariffs on Canadian cheese that used to come in tax-free under the USMCA trade deal. It argues the old law has been quietly replaced by newer laws, and that Canada isn't discriminating anyway: two of Trump's complaints are just Canada answering Trump's own tariffs. It wants the tariffs cancelled and money refunded with interest. Its lawyers, the Liberty Justice Center, won the case where the Supreme Court struck down Trump's 'reciprocal' tariffs in February.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs are paid by importers and often passed on to shoppers as higher prices. If courts keep limiting how presidents can use old laws to set tariffs, it shapes the whole US trade war — including with Canada, the US's close neighbour.
stories.camps: Challengers: "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf," says the Liberty Justice Center; Congress, not the president, should set taxes. The administration's side: Trump says Canada's rules on cars, alcohol and dairy hurt US businesses and that the tariffs are fair payback. The White House did not immediately comment.
stories.image_alt: President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House
stories.image_credit: Photo: Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A tax on goods brought in from another country.
Part of a 1930 US trade law that lets the president tax imports from countries that discriminate against US goods.
A special US federal court that handles cases about imports and tariffs.
The trade deal between the US, Mexico and Canada.
Trump's 2025 tariffs on many countries, meant to match their taxes on US goods. The Supreme Court struck them down.
Money paid back.

stories.headline: Ryanair boss warns European plane tickets could jump up to 20% next year — 'the biggest increase in history'
stories.dek: Jet fuel has soared since the war on Iran began. Many airlines locked in cheap fuel for 2026 but not for 2027. United Airlines also cut its profit forecast.
stories.caveman: Planes run on jet fuel, and it's one of an airline's biggest costs. Since the war on Iran began in late February, fuel supplies have been choked and prices have shot up: the airline group IATA expects jet fuel to average about $152 a barrel in 2026, up from $90 last year. Many European airlines "hedged" — they locked in fuel prices in advance — for this year. Ryanair locked in 80% at $67 a barrel. But Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary says it's 85% unprotected next year, and most rivals are in a similar spot. So he predicts European fares will rise 10%, 15%, maybe 20% in 2027, the biggest jump he's ever seen, and warns some airlines may go bust or get bought. In the US, United Airlines on Tuesday slashed its 2026 profit forecast because of fuel, even though passenger numbers are still up more than 2% and fares are higher.
stories.why_it_matters: If you plan to fly in or around Europe next year, expect to pay more. It also shows how a war far away ends up in everyday prices, from plane tickets to the goods carried by air.
stories.camps: Airline bosses: they say they have no choice — fuel is too expensive to absorb, and weaker airlines will fail. Travellers and consumer groups: surveys show people are braced to pay more, but nobody knows how long families can afford pricier holidays; higher fares also hit people who fly to see relatives or for work.
stories.image_alt: A Ryanair Boeing 737 on the runway at an airport
stories.image_credit: Photo: Alexandros Avramidis/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: The special fuel that airplanes burn.
Paying in advance to lock in a price, so you're protected if prices rise.
The standard unit for oil, about 159 litres.
The International Air Transport Association, the global group for airlines.
A company's guess of how much money it will make.

stories.headline: Netflix beats profit estimates but its stock falls 6% after it lowers its ad-money forecast
stories.dek: Profit jumped to $3.66 billion. But Netflix now expects about $2.7 billion in ad revenue this year instead of $3 billion, and investors worry people are watching less.
stories.caveman: Netflix makes money mostly from subscriptions, plus a cheaper plan with ads. On Tuesday it said profit for July to September was $3.66 billion, up from $2.55 billion a year ago, and revenue grew almost 12%, helped by price rises in March. That beat Wall Street's guesses. But two things worried investors. First, Netflix lowered its full-year ad revenue forecast to about $2.7 billion from about $3 billion, saying some ad tools rolled out slower than planned. Second, its full-year sales forecast of $51.1 billion was at the low end of its range and a bit below expectations. Shares fell about 6% in after-hours trading. Netflix also recently cut about 6% of staff (around 1,000 people) and replaced its top content boss. It admitted "investor concern about our view hours growth" as YouTube and others compete for our eyeballs.
stories.why_it_matters: Netflix is the biggest streaming service, so its numbers tell us how the TV business is changing. A slowdown in watching time and ads could mean more price rises, more ads, or more cost cuts for viewers.
stories.camps: Bulls: profit is growing fast, members keep paying higher prices, and co-CEO Greg Peters says the ad business still has "a long road of continued growth." Bears: viewing hours are flat, YouTube is a fierce rival, the ad plan is behind schedule, and layoffs plus a leadership shake-up raise questions about strategy.
stories.image_alt: The Netflix logo displayed on a screen
stories.image_credit: Photo: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A company's report on how much money it made in a period, usually three months.
All the money a company takes in from sales, before costs.
Buying and selling stocks after the main market closes.
A cheaper subscription plan where you watch some ads.
When a company lets workers go to save money.

stories.headline: Elon Musk says a giant Tesla–SpaceX merger is being seriously considered
stories.dek: Both companies have formed special committees to study it. Together they're valued at about $3.5 trillion. Tesla shareholders would have to approve.
stories.caveman: Elon Musk runs both Tesla (electric cars and robots) and SpaceX (rockets, Starlink internet satellites, and now AI computing). On SpaceX's results call on Tuesday, he said he thinks merging the two "would be a good idea" and that special committees at both companies are studying it. He warned there's no deal on terms yet and "no guarantee" there will be. Tesla is worth about $1.5 trillion and SpaceX about $2 trillion, so it would be one of the biggest mergers ever. SpaceX's fastest-growing business is renting out AI computing power to companies like Anthropic and Google, which brought in $7.5 billion last quarter; Starlink made $5.2 billion. But SpaceX overall has lost $1.1 billion this year. Musk called himself a "conflicted party" because he leads both, and said at least 50% of Tesla shareholders would need to agree. SpaceX shares rose 8% after hours; Tesla rose 2%.
stories.why_it_matters: Musk keeps folding his companies together: SpaceX already swallowed his AI firm xAI and the social network X. One giant company would put even more money and power — in cars, space, internet and AI — under one person.
stories.camps: Supporters: Musk says the companies already share work on chips (a joint project called Terafab), AI and software, so combining them could make both stronger. Critics: when the same person runs both sides, it's hard to make sure each company's shareholders get a fair deal; some also worry about one billionaire controlling so much key technology.
stories.image_alt: Elon Musk, chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX
stories.image_credit: Photo: Courtesy/X via BBC News

terms.explain: When two companies join together to become one.
A small group of independent board members who study a deal when the boss has a conflict of interest.
When a person has two roles whose interests could clash, so it's hard to be fair to both.
People and funds that own a piece of a company and get to vote on big decisions.
SpaceX's internet service that beams internet from thousands of satellites.
Musk's artificial intelligence company, now part of SpaceX.

stories.headline: NPR: TikTok workers warned bosses about child safety for years, court records show — and say leaders failed to act
stories.dek: Staff testimony describes kids appearing in paid sexual livestreams and teens dodging parental controls. TikTok says the claims are 'cherry-picked' by trial lawyers.
stories.caveman: TikTok, along with Meta, Google and Snap, is being sued in a giant set of US lawsuits that say social media apps are designed in ways that harm kids. NPR reviewed staff depositions (sworn interviews) filed in federal court in March 2026 that hadn't been reported before. In them, employees say they raised alarms about children appearing in sexual content on TikTok Live, where viewers send paid "gifts" that can turn into money — meaning TikTok could profit. One internal investigation found kids aged 13 to 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone. A former safety leader, Reagen Maher, said she spent months on a "crusade" to get top executives to act. Staff also flagged that teens used loopholes to get around age limits and block parents from seeing their activity, and records say TikTok avoided surveys of users' ages because it might have to share results with regulators. TikTok has already settled some cases, including $100 million with Alabama.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of kids use TikTok every day. These records suggest the company knew about serious risks, which matters for the lawsuits, for new laws on kids and social media, and for parents deciding what apps their children use.
stories.camps: Critics and families: the testimony shows profit was put ahead of children's safety, and companies won't change unless courts and lawmakers force them. TikTok: a spokesperson said the story uses claims "clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers" to "inaccurately rewrite our history," and points to its published youth-safety policies. The depositions haven't been tested in front of a jury yet.
stories.image_alt: The TikTok logo on a smartphone screen
stories.image_credit: Photo: Imen Ben Youssef/AFP via Getty Images, via NPR

terms.explain: A sworn interview before a trial, where lawyers question a witness and it's written down as evidence.
When many similar lawsuits from around the US are grouped under one judge to save time.
TikTok's live-streaming feature where viewers can send creators paid virtual gifts.
To end a lawsuit by agreeing to pay or change things, without a trial verdict.
Federal Trade Commission, the US agency that protects consumers, including kids' privacy online.
Settings that let parents limit or see what their kids do on an app.

stories.headline: Salesforce agrees to buy marketing-app maker Braze for $5.66 billion; Braze stock rockets 51%
stories.dek: Salesforce will pay $47.50 a share in cash. It's the latest AI shopping spree for the business-software giant, months after it bought customer-service AI firm Fin.
stories.caveman: Salesforce makes software that companies use to keep track of their customers. On Tuesday it agreed to buy Braze, a company whose AI tools help brands manage customer data and send messages — like app notifications, emails and texts. Salesforce will pay $47.50 in cash for each Braze share, which values the deal at about $5.66 billion. Braze shares closed at $30.04 the day before, so investors rushed in: the stock jumped more than 51% to $45.57. The deal still needs approval from shareholders and regulators and is expected to close in Salesforce's fiscal 2028. Braze CEO Bill Magnuson said Braze will keep building its product inside Salesforce. Earlier this year Salesforce agreed to buy AI customer-service platform Fin for about $3.6 billion, and in August it expanded a partnership with Anthropic.
stories.why_it_matters: Big software companies are racing to buy AI tools so businesses can automate marketing and customer service. That could mean smarter (or more frequent) messages to you as a shopper, and fewer independent tech companies.
stories.camps: Supporters: Salesforce says combining forces helps marketers build better relationships with customers and lets Braze innovate faster. Skeptics: each big purchase concentrates more customer data in a few giant companies, and regulators may look closely; some investors also question whether Salesforce is paying too much in the AI rush.
stories.image_alt: The Salesforce cloud logo at a company booth
stories.image_credit: Photo: Sheldon Cooper/LightRocket/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: When one company buys another.
For each single share of stock.
Ways companies keep in touch with customers, like app alerts, emails and texts.
Government agencies that check whether big deals are fair and legal.
AI that can take actions on its own, like answering customers or updating records.

stories.headline: Judge dismisses Ann Altman's sexual abuse lawsuit against her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman
stories.dek: The judge said she refused to attend a required independent medical exam despite warnings. Sam Altman has denied the accusations.
stories.caveman: In January 2025, Ann Altman sued her brother Sam Altman, the head of ChatGPT maker OpenAI, in federal court in St. Louis, Missouri. She accused him of repeatedly sexually abusing her between 1997 and 2006, starting when she was 3 and he was 12. Sam Altman has denied it. On Tuesday, US district judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the case. He wrote that she refused to show up for an independent medical examination, even after being warned that not going would end the case. Her current lawyer did not immediately comment; a former lawyer who withdrew this month said he still believes in her. The Altman family has said Ann has mental health challenges and has received financial support, and Sam Altman has said the accusations began after the family turned down her demands for more money.
stories.why_it_matters: Altman leads one of the world's most powerful AI companies, so the case drew wide attention. The dismissal was about a court procedure — not a finding that the abuse did or didn't happen.
stories.camps: Sam Altman's side: he has consistently denied the claims, and the family says Ann's accusations followed money disputes. Ann Altman's supporters: her former lawyer says he still believes her, and survivor advocates note that abuse cases are often hard to bring years later and that a procedural dismissal doesn't settle the facts. If you or someone you know needs help in the US, the Childhelp hotline is 800-422-4453.
stories.image_alt: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks at UN headquarters in New York
stories.image_credit: Photo: Lev Radin/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: When a judge ends a lawsuit before a full trial.
A check-up by a doctor chosen to be neutral, often required when someone claims harm in a lawsuit.
A judge in a US federal trial court.
About the rules of how a case must be run, not about who is right on the facts.
The company behind ChatGPT.

stories.headline: Alberta votes about 76% to 24% to stay in Canada, crushing a push to start leaving
stories.dek: The oil-rich province rejected beginning a separation process in a referendum. PM Mark Carney cheered; separatists say a quarter of voters still feel badly treated.
stories.caveman: Alberta is a big, oil-rich province in western Canada. Many people there feel the national government in Ottawa ignores them. On Monday, Albertans voted on 10 questions, including whether to start a legal process that could lead to a second vote on leaving Canada. With nearly 1.9 million votes counted, about 76% said stay and 24% said start separating, according to unofficial results. Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Alberta's capital Edmonton, said "Albertans chose Canada." Alberta premier Danielle Smith, who allowed the vote, welcomed the result too. A separatist leader, Keith Wilson, said at least a quarter of Albertans want better treatment. Others in the movement called it a clear defeat. A radio host grumbled that the vote cost taxpayers $130m. Some results on the other questions, like immigration and healthcare, could take days.
stories.why_it_matters: A breakup of Canada would have shaken North America. The result gives Carney a stronger hand as he faces pressure from US President Trump, including tariffs — but the anger behind the vote hasn't gone away.
stories.camps: Unity side: pollster David Coletto says most Albertans have deep complaints about Ottawa but are "proudly Canadian" and saw the vote as a distraction from bigger threats like the Trump administration. Separatists: they say the ballot question was unfair and that a quarter of voters wanting change is a message Ottawa must hear.
stories.image_alt: Supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign wearing Canadian flags cheer at a watch party in Edmonton
stories.image_credit: Photo: Canadian Press/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: A vote where all citizens decide one specific question directly.
A big region of Canada with its own government, a bit like a US state.
Someone who wants their region to break away and become its own country.
The leader of a Canadian province's government.
Canada's capital; often used to mean the national government.
Early vote counts that haven't been formally confirmed yet.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says US intelligence sharing on Russian missiles 'works now' after talks with Trump's envoy in Oslo
stories.dek: Envoy Steve Witkoff heads to meet Putin in Russia today with the new proposals. Trump keeps telling Ukraine to 'make a deal'.
stories.caveman: Ukraine says it needs US spy information to get early warnings when Russian missiles are coming. Last week Kyiv accused Washington of holding some back; US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called that claim "scandalous". On Tuesday in Oslo, Norway, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, with Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joining by video. Afterward Zelenskyy said he is "thankful that intelligence works now" because early warnings save civilians, and he hopes to fix speed limits Ukraine's military has noticed on SpaceX's Starlink. Stubb said there was "genuine progress" on peace proposals but gave no details. A US official called the talks "very productive". Witkoff is due to meet Vladimir Putin in Russia on Wednesday. Russia's foreign minister said Moscow will listen but rules out "any political concessions". Russian drones killed at least 10 people in Ukraine on Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022 and Moscow holds about 20% of Ukraine. Whether the US keeps helping Ukraine, and on what terms a ceasefire might come, affects millions of lives and Europe's security.
stories.camps: Ukraine and Europe: they say the ball is now in Russia's court and that early warnings and air defence are matters of life and death. Trump: he says Russia wants to "get it done", that it's "time for Ukraine to end this war," and has blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries for higher fuel prices. Some Republicans in Congress have pushed back on his wavering support for Kyiv.
stories.image_alt: Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy before talks in Oslo
stories.image_credit: Photo: Reuters via BBC News

terms.explain: When one country gives another secret information, like spy satellite data about incoming missiles.
A person sent by a leader to negotiate on their behalf.
An alert that a missile or drone is coming, so people can take shelter.
Things one side gives up to reach a deal.
Russia's seat of government in Moscow; often means Putin's government.
An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a while.

stories.headline: Europe's cost-of-living unrest spreads: Italy sends 500 troops to Milan, and France will use soldiers to guard sites this weekend
stories.dek: Milan police detained 271 young people after looting near the cathedral. France, with nearly 2,400 arrests last weekend, keeps curfews in parts of Paris and plans a 'massive' police presence Saturday.
stories.caveman: Across Europe, people are angry about high prices and worse public services. Last weekend, mostly peaceful marches in France and Italy turned violent at the edges. In Milan, hooded youths set bins on fire, smashed windows and looted shops around the cathedral; police used teargas and water cannon and detained 271 young people. Luxury brands like Chanel and Dior emptied their shop windows. Italy's far-right government under Giorgia Meloni is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and proposing a new crime of violent participation in a protest, tougher penalties, and making parents pay for damage their kids cause. In France, where nearly 2,400 people were arrested and Limoges' historic town hall was burned, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said soldiers from the anti-terror force Sentinelle will guard buildings so police can focus on keeping order. Curfews were renewed in parts of Paris. More protests are planned for Saturday in both countries.
stories.why_it_matters: When governments answer protests with soldiers and new crimes, it raises big questions about public safety versus the right to protest. France also has a debt problem and a presidential election in April 2027, so unrest could reshape politics.
stories.camps: Governments: Italy promises a "firm response from the state"; France wants "an immediate return to order" and business groups say 3,000+ shops were sacked. Critics and protesters: most marchers were peaceful and are angry about real costs of living; rights groups worry about heavy-handed policing (French police were accused of excessive force after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off by a stun grenade), and some measures in Italy target immigrant youth.
stories.image_alt: Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan
stories.image_credit: Photo: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: How much money people need for basics like food, rent, energy and transport.
A rule that people must stay off the streets during certain hours.
Stealing from shops during chaos or riots.
A French military operation, created after the 2015 Paris attacks, that puts soldiers on patrol at home.
Politics strongly focused on nationalism, strict immigration limits and law and order.
A gas that stings the eyes, used by police to scatter crowds.

stories.headline: Two weeks before US midterms, Trump says he'll spend $400m helping Republicans while Michael Bloomberg gives $80m to Democrats
stories.dek: Democrats hope to flip the narrowly-held House and maybe the Senate on Nov. 3, but trail in fundraising. Elon Musk has spent $366m on conservative groups.
stories.caveman: US midterm elections happen halfway through a president's term; this year voting day is Nov. 3. All seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate are up. Republicans control the House by a tiny margin. On Tuesday, President Trump said he plans to spend $400 million to help Republican candidates, with $300 million already given out. The same day, the New York Times reported that billionaire and former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg, 84, gave about $80 million to help Democrats in September and October, including $24 million to the gun-safety group Everytown and $16 million to the House Majority PAC. His adviser said the goal is a big House majority, not just the 218 seats needed. Democrats admit they've raised less money than Republicans, who are also helped by Elon Musk's $366 million.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever controls Congress decides which laws pass and whether Trump's government faces investigations. The flood of money from a few very rich people raises questions about how much influence billionaires have over elections.
stories.camps: Democrats: they believe they're favoured to win the House and have a shot at the four Senate seats they need; Bloomberg's money helps close the gap. Republicans: Trump's huge war chest and Musk's spending show strong support for his agenda. Good-government groups on both sides worry that elections increasingly depend on a handful of billionaires.
stories.image_alt: Former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg speaking at an event
stories.image_credit: Photo: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, for Congress and many state jobs.
The bigger chamber of Congress, with 435 members; 218 is a majority.
The smaller chamber of Congress, with 100 members; it also approves judges.
Political action committee: a group that raises and spends money to help candidates.
To win a seat or chamber from the other party.
A big pile of money saved up for a campaign.

stories.headline: HOT: Meet the seven debut novelists up for the Center for Fiction's First Novel Prize
stories.dek: Lit Hub interviews the finalists, including T Kira Madden (Whidbey) and Nafissa Thompson-Spires. The $15,000 winner is announced in December.
stories.caveman: A debut novel is a writer's first novel. The Center for Fiction, a New York literary non-profit, gives one of America's best-known prizes for debuts. This year's seven finalists are Emeline Atwood (A Real Animal), Samantha Josephs (Carrying), T Kira Madden (Whidbey), Giada Scodellaro (Ruins, Child), Avigayl Sharp (Offseason), Ankur Thakkar (Blow Yourself Up), and Nafissa Thompson-Spires (The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford). The judges are well-known writers R. O. Kwon, Kiese Laymon, Jordy Rosenberg and Danzy Senna. Each finalist gets $1,000; the winner, named in December, gets $15,000. Literary Hub asked them about their writing lives. One finalist confesses she's trying to wake up at 6am with help from her chihuahua; tips for writer's block include writing what you wish had happened yesterday. Advice quoted includes Ira Glass on the "gap" between your taste and your early work, and Ursula K. Le Guin on dragons.
stories.why_it_matters: Debut prizes are how new names break through. If you want to know which young American novelists critics are watching right now, this shortlist is a good reading list.
stories.camps: Fans: shortlists like this spotlight fresh, diverse voices that big marketing budgets might miss. Skeptics: prizes can feel like an insiders' club in New York publishing, and a shortlist only reflects a few judges' tastes — plenty of great debuts never make one.
stories.image_alt: Covers of the seven shortlisted debut novels for the Center for Fiction First Novel Prize
stories.image_credit: Image: Literary Hub / The Center for Fiction

terms.explain: An author's first published novel.
The final small group of books still in the running for a prize.
A New York non-profit that supports readers and writers of fiction.
When a writer feels stuck and can't get words onto the page.
A popular US website about books and writing, often called Lit Hub.

stories.headline: HOT: YA author Mindy McGinnis says her first horror novel, 'What Rough Beast', is really about everyday sexism
stories.dek: In a Publishers Weekly essay, the Edgar Award winner explains how small 'just joking' moments add up to misogyny — and why her heroine gets punished for calling them out.
stories.caveman: YA means "young adult": books written for teenagers. Mindy McGinnis, who won the Edgar Award (a top mystery prize) for A Madness So Discreet, has a new teen novel, What Rough Beast (HarperCollins, out Oct. 27). It's her first book with a supernatural monster. Its heroine, Ava, lives in the rural Midwest and is shunned after she calls out sexist behaviour; the backlash wakes "an ancient evil" underground. In an essay for Publishers Weekly, McGinnis writes that sexism shows up in all her books without her planning it, because it's how women and girls move through the world. She describes a family Christmas party where her father was gifted a swimsuit calendar and the men joked about it; she was the only one who objected and was told she was "overreacting." A male friend who read an early copy texted her that it made him lose sleep thinking about how he treated women when he was younger.
stories.why_it_matters: Horror is a popular way for writers to talk about real fears. Books like this give teens, and adults, a way to discuss consent, sexism and speaking up.
stories.camps: Fans: readers and critics praise YA that tackles hard topics honestly, and McGinnis has a long track record on assault, addiction and mental health. Critics of the trend: some parents and school boards object to dark or mature themes in teen books, and a few readers prefer horror that's just scary rather than a social message.
stories.image_alt: Author Mindy McGinnis and the cover of her novel What Rough Beast
stories.image_credit: Image: Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: Young adult: books written mainly for teenagers.
Dislike of, or prejudice against, women and girls.
A major US prize for mystery and crime writing.
Involving ghosts, monsters or forces beyond normal science.
Small, everyday comments or actions that put down a group of people, often without meaning to.

stories.headline: NOT: Palestinian American authors pull their kids' history book from Random House after a fight over edits
stories.dek: Jenan A. Matari and Alana Hadid say the publisher added language they never wrote about October 7. The book will now come out with Palestinian-owned indie press Interlink in 2027.
stories.caveman: Displacement and the Palestinian American Story was supposed to be the seventh book in Random House Children's Books' "Race to the Truth" series, nonfiction for ages 10 and up told by writers from marginalised communities. It was due Sept. 29. The co-authors, Jenan A. Matari and Alana Hadid, say a June 2026 version of the manuscript included a line they did not write calling the events of October 7, 2023, a "violation of international law," mixed up the words "Jewish" and "Zionist," and reordered chapters so the timeline no longer made sense. Advance copies had already gone out. After months of talks, the publisher offered more edits, raising the age range to 14+, or adding a publisher's note; the authors refused and cancelled the contract in September. Random House says it gave guidance so young first-time readers had enough context, and that it supports the authors publishing elsewhere. Retitled Understanding Palestine for Young Readers, the book is now due from Interlink Books in summer 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how hard it is for big US publishers to handle the Israel–Palestine conflict, especially in books for kids. Who gets to tell a community's history, and how, is a hot debate in publishing.
stories.camps: The authors and series co-founder Saira Rao: they say the book faced scrutiny no other title in the series got, and that a Black author writing about slavery would never be asked to add such a clause. Random House: it says the edits aimed to help 10-year-olds understand a complex subject, it offered several compromises, and it "would not move forward with a book that the authors were not comfortable publishing."
stories.image_alt: Coauthors Jenan A. Matari and Alana Hadid
stories.image_credit: Image: Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: The text of a book before it's printed.
Early versions of a book sent to reviewers before it goes on sale.
A supporter of Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state in Israel. Not the same as being Jewish.
The October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, which started the Gaza war.
A small independent publisher, not owned by a big corporation.
When the right to publish a book goes back from the publisher to the author.

stories.headline: HOT: This week's big new books are nonfiction — Meghan O'Rourke's illness poems, Lawrence Wright on sisterhood and justice, and 'Anti-Fascist Economics'
stories.dek: Lit Hub's Tuesday list of 20 new releases says the giant fall fiction rush is easing and serious nonfiction is taking over.
stories.caveman: Every Tuesday, US publishers release new books, and Literary Hub rounds up the most interesting. After "one of the biggest fiction falls" ever, this week leans nonfiction. Highlights: poet Meghan O'Rourke's The Story of the Body: Poems of Illness and Recovery (Norton), which writer Ocean Vuong calls "essential reading for all"; Pulitzer winner Lawrence Wright's Redemption: Faith, Justice, and Sisterhood (Knopf); economist Isabella Weber's Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defense of Affordability, Dignity, and Democracy (Random House), praised by former FTC chair Lina Khan; Paris Marx's Hyperscale, about Big Tech's giant data centres (Riverhead); and Thomas Frank's The Creativity Con, on how "innovation" talk hides inequality (Penguin Press). Fiction picks include K-Ming Chang's Needlemouth (Simon & Schuster). Also out: Zaina Arafat's Our Arab and J. Vanessa Lyon's memoir Blackness Thirteen Ways.
stories.why_it_matters: This list is a snapshot of what American readers are thinking about right now: health, justice, the cost of living, and the power of tech giants — the same topics in the news.
stories.camps: Fans: it's a rich week for readers who like books that explain the world, with big names and fresh voices side by side. Skeptics: the titles lean heavily political and serious; some readers say they want escape, and these weekly lists can feel like a marketing parade rather than real criticism.
stories.image_alt: Detail of a classical painting showing two shirtless men, used as the lead image for Lit Hub's new-releases list
stories.image_credit: Image: Literary Hub

terms.explain: Books about real people, events and ideas, not made-up stories.
The day a book goes on sale; in the US, it's usually Tuesday.
A true story an author writes about their own life.
A top US award for journalism, books and music.
A short quote of praise printed on or about a book, often from another writer.

stories.headline: Sudan army drone strikes reportedly kill more than 300 people, including mourners on a truck and shoppers at a fuel market
stories.dek: A monitor says 150 died in West Kordofan on Sunday; officials in disputed Abyei say 153 died when a market was hit Monday. South Sudan has protested.
stories.caveman: Since 2023, Sudan's army and a paramilitary group called the RSF have been fighting a war for control of the country. Both now use drones, often supplied by foreign countries despite a partial arms embargo. The monitoring group Sudan War Observatory says army drones on Sunday evening hit a truck carrying about 200 mourners arriving for a funeral in Al-Dabab, West Kordofan, killing 145, plus five more in a funeral tent; a market in Al-Mujlad was also bombed. On Monday, drones hit Amiet Market near Abyei town, a disputed area jointly run by Sudan and South Sudan. The region's information minister says 153 people died. A military source told the BBC the army did the Abyei strike because the market supplied fuel to the RSF. The army says it does not attack civilians. BBC Verify found satellite images of burnt buildings at the market. South Sudan summoned Sudan's ambassador.
stories.why_it_matters: Sudan has one of the world's worst humanitarian crises: hundreds of thousands killed, more than 14 million forced from their homes and 20 million facing acute hunger. Attacks near the South Sudan border risk widening the war.
stories.camps: UN and aid groups: UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said he is "alarmed" by drone strikes killing civilians, including children, and disrupting essential services. Sudan's army: it hasn't commented on the Kordofan claims, says it doesn't target civilians, and says the Abyei market was an RSF fuel supply site. Both the army and the RSF have been accused of abuses.
stories.image_alt: People wounded in the attack on Amiet market are treated at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei
stories.image_credit: Photo: MSF via Reuters, via BBC News

terms.explain: Rapid Support Forces, a powerful paramilitary group fighting Sudan's army since 2023.
An armed group organised like an army but not the official national army.
An oil-rich border area claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan.
A ban on selling weapons to a country or group.
A disaster where huge numbers of people lack food, water, safety or shelter.
The BBC team that checks videos, photos and satellite images to confirm what really happened.

stories.headline: Ebola reaches Nigeria's capital as a woman arriving from Uganda tests positive; outbreak is now the most widespread on record
stories.dek: Health officials are tracing 44 contacts in Abuja. Kenya has nine cases. Africa CDC calls it 'an extremely serious threat' with a death rate near 50%.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a rare but deadly virus that spreads through contact with an infected person's body fluids. On Tuesday, Nigeria confirmed its first case of this outbreak: a woman who arrived in the capital, Abuja, from Uganda. She got sick on Oct. 7 and went to a private hospital on Oct. 11. Health Minister Muhammad Pate said officials are tracing 44 people she had contact with. This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain. It started in Congo in mid-May and has infected more than 9,000 people and killed more than 4,300. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and now has nine. Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya says it's already the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history, across three regions of Africa. The WHO says it's the fastest-spreading on record and could pass the 2014–16 West Africa outbreak, which killed 11,000. Vaccines like Ervebo are being given in Congo.
stories.why_it_matters: Abuja is a big, busy city with flights all over the world, so a case there raises fears of wider spread. Fast contact tracing and isolation are the best tools to stop it.
stories.camps: Nigerian officials: they set up an Ebola task force in June and say surveillance, isolation and lab testing are ready, to avoid a repeat of 2014 when a traveller brought the virus in. Health experts: the speed and spread are alarming, and aid cuts and weak health systems in some countries make it harder to stop outbreaks early.
stories.image_alt: A health worker gives a dose of Ervebo Ebola vaccine in Beni, eastern Congo
stories.image_credit: Photo: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP via NPR

terms.explain: A severe, often deadly virus that causes fever and bleeding and spreads through body fluids.
Finding everyone a sick person was near, so they can be checked and kept from spreading the disease.
One type (strain) of the Ebola virus, named after a district in Uganda.
The African Union's public health agency.
The share of infected people who die.
The World Health Organization, the UN's health agency.

stories.headline: Guardian investigation: In Louisiana, small-town judges get paid from eviction fees — and one earned more than the US chief justice
stories.dek: Justice of the peace Chuck Cusimano II made over $400,000 in 2025. His court ordered 3,276 evictions in a year and ruled for tenants in only 141 cases.
stories.caveman: An eviction is when a landlord goes to court to force a tenant out of their home. In most of Louisiana, landlords can file eviction cases in "justice of the peace" courts. These judges don't need a law degree — just good moral character, a high school diploma and the ability to write English correctly. Uniquely in the US, experts say, their pay depends directly on how many fees they collect, and landlords pay those fees and choose which court to use. The Guardian found these courts collected $45 million in fees over 10 years, and justices kept at least an estimated $31 million as personal pay. Justice Chuck Cusimano II, who sits part-time in suburban Jefferson parish, earned more than $400,000 in 2025, over $80,000 more than Chief Justice John Roberts. From June 2025 to May 2026 his court handled more than 5,500 eviction cases; almost one in five renter households in his district faced eviction.
stories.why_it_matters: Losing a home can push families into debt, job loss and homelessness. If a judge earns more when more landlords file cases, critics say tenants may not get a fair hearing.
stories.camps: Critics: a class-action lawsuit says the fee system pushes judges to favour landlords; a former US Justice Department official called it "blatantly unconstitutional," and experts say courts should be paid from general taxes. The judge and the state: Cusimano says there's no conflict because landlords pay up front "irrespective of the outcome," and his district simply has lots of apartments; Louisiana's attorney general says these justices "play a vital role."
stories.image_alt: A constable knocks on a door to deliver an eviction notice in Jefferson parish, Louisiana
stories.image_credit: Photo: Annie Flanagan/The Guardian

terms.explain: When a landlord legally forces a tenant to leave their home.
A local, part-time judge who handles small cases like evictions and minor claims.
A person who rents a home.
A lawsuit filed on behalf of a large group of people with the same complaint.
When someone could gain personally from a decision they're supposed to make fairly.
Louisiana's word for a county.

stories.headline: Giving Indigenous families in Peru's Amazon about £2 a day, no strings attached, helped protect the rainforest, study finds
stories.dek: Almost 90% of people in the pilot adopted greener practices like replanting. Hunger and forced migration dropped sharply. Researchers say bigger studies are still needed.
stories.caveman: A "basic income" means giving people regular cash they can spend however they want. A UK charity, Cool Earth, ran a two-year pilot with 211 Asháninka Indigenous people in three communities in Peru's Amazon. Each got six payments of 1,032 Peruvian soles, roughly £2 a day. The project was designed with local women's groups. A University of Bath study found almost 90% of participants took up environment-friendly practices, like replanting forest together, restoring water sources and burning less forest. Households that couldn't afford healthy food fell from 73% to 26%, and the share of people forced to leave home to find work fell from 43% to 18%, so more people stayed to look after the forest. The researchers say it's the first unconditional basic income given to an Indigenous community in the Amazon.
stories.why_it_matters: The Amazon stores huge amounts of carbon and is home to countless species. Indigenous people are among its best protectors, but they face miners, loggers and poverty. Direct cash could be a respectful, simple way to support them.
stories.camps: Supporters: co-author Nick Langridge says communities with more security and autonomy protect their ecosystems better, and lead author Neil Howard says it treats people with dignity, unlike colonial-style conservation. Cautious experts: other studies found cash can increase deforestation if people expand farms or buy vehicles that bring more roads; this study was small (about 500 hectares) and didn't measure the forest itself.
stories.image_alt: Aerial view of a river winding through the rainforest in Peru's Asháninka region
stories.image_credit: Photo: Martín Mejía/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: Regular cash payments given to people with no conditions on how to spend it.
The original peoples of a land, who lived there before colonisers arrived.
An Indigenous people living in the rainforests of Peru and Brazil.
A small first test of an idea before trying it on a bigger scale.
Cutting down or burning forests, usually for farms, roads or wood.
Not having reliable access to enough healthy food.
